key_insight: Microscopic residual impurities in wide-bandgap perovskite films are not just defects—they are chemically active failure nuclei that trigger early degradation at impurity–perovskite interfaces.
engineering_relevance: A fast, non-invasive microscopy-plus-ML screening workflow can pre-qualify perovskite films by impurity density before module-scale processing, improving stability and manufacturability.
method: Nano-FTIR to chemically identify impurity species in perovskite films
High-resolution reflected-light microscopy for rapid, non-invasive imaging
Machine-learning image analysis to detect and quantify harmful impurities within seconds
evidence_signal: Photo-stress and degradation-tracking experiments showed that films with higher impurity density degraded faster, and degradation consistently initiated at impurity–perovskite interfaces.
watch_item: The screening metric is promising, but its robustness likely depends on imaging quality, calibration, and transferability across different perovskite compositions and fabrication lines.
paper_title: High-Throughput Imaging of Degradation-Inducing Microscopic Impurities in Perovskite Solar Cells
